summary.text: The cell cycle is the sequence of events in a cell that leads to its division into two daughter cells.
In eukaryotic cells it has two main stages: interphase, when the cell grows and replicates its DNA, and the M phase, which includes mitosis and cytokinesis.
Checkpoints follow each key stage of the cycle and control whether the cell moves on to the next.

facts.label: Interphase share
facts.value: Typically at least 91% of the total cycle time

facts.label: DNA copying
facts.value: Nuclear DNA is duplicated during S phase

facts.label: Resting state
facts.value: G₀ is where a cell has stopped dividing

facts.label: Prokaryote periods
facts.value: Bacteria and archaea use B, C and D periods

items.prompt: If you looked at a growing population of eukaryotic cells at random, which stage would most of them be in?

options.label: M phase, since that is when everything happens
Mitosis, since it is the longest part of the cycle
Cytokinesis, since cells wait a long time to split
Interphase, which takes most of the total cycle time

items.explain: Interphase typically lasts for at least 91% of the total time required for the cell cycle.

items.prompt: A neuron may stop dividing for years, or even permanently. What is this resting state called?

options.label: S phase, the stage of DNA synthesis
G₀ phase, a quiescent state entered from G₁
M phase, the stage of nuclear division
G₂ phase, the second gap before division

items.explain: Non-dividing cells in multicellular eukaryotes generally enter the quiescent G₀ state from G₁ and may stay there indefinitely, as is often the case for neurons.

items.prompt: A scrape on the skin heals over. What role does the cell cycle play in that?

options.label: Repeated rounds of cell division regenerate and heal the skin
Cells enter G₀ so that they can grow into replacement skin
Skin cells repair themselves without ever dividing again
Skin cells skip interphase and divide immediately

items.explain: In multicellular organisms a series of cell-division cycles is the process by which skin, hair and blood cells are regenerated and healed.

items.prompt: A cell has just finished DNA synthesis. How does each of its chromosomes look now?

options.label: A single chromatid, just as before
Half a chromosome, split down the middle
Two sister chromatids joined together
Two separate chromosomes in different nuclei

items.explain: When S phase is complete, all of the chromosomes have been replicated, so each one consists of two sister chromatids.

items.prompt: A cell passes the G₁ checkpoint known as the restriction point. What does passing it mean?

options.label: The cell stops dividing and starts to rest in G₀
The cell is now committed to dividing
The cell must start over from the M phase
The cell can no longer grow in size at all

items.explain: Passage through the G₁ checkpoint commits the cell to division.

items.prompt: Suppose a cell does not properly complete one phase of the cycle. What does that mean for the phase that follows?

options.label: The next phase starts anyway, one step behind
The next phase starts early to make up the time
The next phase is skipped, and the cycle moves on
The next phase cannot be properly activated

items.explain: Activation of each phase depends on the proper progression and completion of the previous one.
